cards.explanation: The answer is True, friends. The text says Zedekiah "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done." (2 Kings 24:19) Jehoiakim was an earlier king of Judah, and the writer sets the two kings side by side. I think that's a heavy thing to read.

The answer is that he rebels, friends. The text says "…Zedekiah also rebelled against the king of Babylon." (2 Kings 24:20) This is the same king of Babylon who put him on the throne (2 Kings 24:17). That's like biting the hand that handed you the crown. I think even my mustache would've said, "Maybe not."

The answer is wall, friends. The army "…encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it." (2 Kings 25:1) All around means the wall circles the whole city. It's like walking out your front door and finding a wall where your driveway used to be.

The answer is False, friends. The text says "…the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food." (2 Kings 25:3) That's where a long siege ends up. I think this is a hungry, heavy stretch for the people inside, so I'll keep my jokes in the oven.

The answer is that they flee by night, friends! The text says "…all the men of war fled by night by way of the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden." (2 Kings 25:4) They headed toward the Arabah, even though the Chaldeans, Babylon's army, had surrounded the city.

The answer is that they chase after them, friends. The text says "…the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plains of Jericho…" (2 Kings 25:5) The men of war left by night, but the Chaldeans went after the king and caught him. His whole army deserted him.

The answer is False, friends. The text says the Chaldeans overtook the king "…and his whole army deserted him." (2 Kings 25:5) Not part of the army, the whole army. I think that's a lonely moment, so I'll let it sit.

The answer is Riblah, friends! The Chaldeans "…brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where they pronounced judgment on him." (2 Kings 25:6) Riblah shows up again later in this passage, when others are brought there too (2 Kings 25:20). It's a name worth remembering.

The answer is to Babylon, friends. The text says they "…put out his eyes, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon." (2 Kings 25:7) I think this is one of the heaviest verses in the passage, so I'm not joking here. Zedekiah goes to the very land of the king he rebelled against.

The answer is that he burns it down, friends. The text says "He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem…" (2 Kings 25:9) I think this one hurts, because it's the house of the LORD. It's a heavy moment, and I won't joke about it.

The answer is False, friends. The text says Nebuzaradan "…burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem…" (2 Kings 25:9) The palace and the houses are on the list right alongside the house of the LORD. I think this is a heavy one.

The answer is that he carries them into exile, friends. The text says Nebuzaradan "…carried into exile the people who remained in the city, along with the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon and the rest of the population." (2 Kings 25:11) The people leave Jerusalem for a far-off land. I think that's a heavy goodbye to a hometown.

The answer is poorest, friends! The text says the captain of the guard "…left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields." (2 Kings 25:12) Some stay behind to work the land. The text doesn't say why, so I won't guess.

The answer is priests and doorkeepers, friends. Nebuzaradan "…took away Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest of second rank, and the three doorkeepers." (2 Kings 25:18) Seraiah is the chief priest, and Zephaniah ranks second. The people who served at the house of the LORD are carried off along with its treasure.

The answer is True, friends. The text says "So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land." (2 Kings 25:21) It's a sad ending to this part of the story. I think that's a lot to carry, so I won't joke.
